```{r setup}
library(multisiteDGP)
```

The standard errors of a simulated data set come from one of two places.
`sim_multisite()` draws a size for each site and derives the standard error
from it. `sim_meta()` sets the standard errors directly, from a target
informativeness and a target ratio of the largest to the smallest sampling
variance.

## Standard errors from site sizes

Six arguments of `sim_multisite()` determine the standard errors. Three
describe the site sizes. The other three set the constant that turns a site
size into a sampling variance.

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|---------------|------------------------------------------------------|-----|
| `nj_mean` | mean site size | 50 |
| `cv` | coefficient of variation of the site sizes (0 gives equal sizes) | 0.5 |
| `nj_min` | smallest site size allowed | 5 |
| `p` | proportion of each site assigned to treatment | 0.5 |
| `R2` | share of the outcome variance explained by covariates | 0 |
| `var_outcome` | variance of the outcome | 1 |

The sampling variance of a site is that of a difference in means between its
$p\,n_j$ treated and $(1 - p)\,n_j$ control individuals. It is a constant
$\kappa$ divided by the site size $n_j$:

$$
\mathrm{se}_j^2 = \frac{\kappa}{n_j}, \qquad
\kappa = \left(\frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{1 - p}\right) (1 - R^2)\, \sigma_Y^2 .
$$

Here $R^2$ is `R2` and $\sigma_Y^2$ is `var_outcome`. `compute_kappa()`
returns $\kappa$.

```{r kappa}
compute_kappa()
compute_kappa(R2 = 0.4)
compute_kappa(p = 0.3)
```

With the defaults $\kappa$ is 4, so a site of 100 individuals has a sampling
variance of 0.04 and a standard error of 0.2. Covariates that explain 40
percent of the outcome variance lower $\kappa$ to 2.4. Treating 30 percent of
each site instead of half raises it from 4 to 4.76. The next call simulates
50 sites with `R2 = 0.4`.

```{r from-sizes}
dat <- sim_multisite(
  J = 50, nj_mean = 50, cv = 0.5, nj_min = 10, R2 = 0.4, seed = 1
)
dat
```

The `n_j` column holds the simulated sizes, and `se2_j` is 2.4 divided by
`n_j`. Site 4 has 12 individuals, a sampling variance of 0.2, and a standard
error of 0.447. Site 6 has 68 individuals and a standard error of 0.188.

```{r sizes-check}
summary(dat$n_j)
range(dat$se2_j * dat$n_j)
```

The 50 sizes run from 12 to 122 and average 49.06, against an `nj_mean` of 50.
The product of `se2_j` and `n_j` is 2.4 for every site.

## The two site-size generators

`sim_multisite()` passes the size arguments to `gen_site_sizes()`, which draws
the sizes with one of two generators. The `engine` argument selects one.

- `engine = "truncated_gamma"`, the default, draws from a gamma distribution
  truncated below at `nj_min`. It solves for the two gamma parameters that
  give the truncated distribution the mean `nj_mean` and the coefficient of
  variation `cv`. Each draw is then rounded down or up at random, which keeps
  the mean and adds a little variance. The site sizes therefore vary slightly
  more than `cv`, most visibly when `cv` is small.
- `engine = "censored"` draws from a gamma distribution with mean `nj_mean`
  and coefficient of variation `cv`, and raises every draw below `nj_min` to
  `nj_min`. This is the procedure of Lee et al. [-@lee2025improving], kept to
  reproduce that paper. The presets `preset_jebs_paper()` and
  `preset_jebs_strict()` use it.

`gen_site_sizes()` can be called on its own, on the output of `gen_effects()`.
The example draws 100,000 sizes, enough to show their distribution, and
raises `nj_min` to 20.

```{r size-step}
set.seed(1)
effects <- gen_effects(J = 100000)
tg <- gen_site_sizes(effects, J = 100000, nj_mean = 50, cv = 0.5, nj_min = 20)
print(tg, n = 3)
```

The function returns the site effects with the columns `n_j`, `se2_j`, and
`se_j` added. The same call with `engine = "censored"` uses the other
generator.

```{r generators}
cens <- gen_site_sizes(
  effects, J = 100000, nj_mean = 50, cv = 0.5, nj_min = 20, engine = "censored"
)
describe <- function(n) round(c(mean = mean(n), cv = sd(n) / mean(n)), 3)
rbind(truncated_gamma = describe(tg$n_j), censored = describe(cens$n_j))
```

The truncated-gamma sizes have a mean of 49.896 and a coefficient of variation
of 0.498, the requested 50 and 0.5 up to sampling error. The censored sizes
have a larger mean (50.345) and a smaller coefficient of variation (0.486).

```{r generator-figure, fig.cap = "The censored sizes have a spike at the minimum of 20, and the truncated-gamma sizes do not."}
library(ggplot2)
sizes <- rbind(
  data.frame(generator = "truncated_gamma", n_j = tg$n_j),
  data.frame(generator = "censored", n_j = cens$n_j)
)
ggplot(sizes, aes(n_j)) +
  geom_bar(aes(y = after_stat(prop)), width = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~generator, ncol = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(20, 150)) +
  labs(x = "site size", y = "share of sites") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The spike holds the draws that fell below 20. Its size depends on how much of
the untruncated gamma distribution lies below `nj_min`.

```{r below-minimum}
pgamma(c(10, 20), shape = 1 / 0.5^2, rate = 1 / (0.5^2 * 50))
```

With a mean of 50 and a coefficient of variation of 0.5, 7.9 percent of the
draws fall below 20 and 0.9 percent fall below 10. With `nj_min = 10` the two
generators draw from almost the same distribution.

For a given ratio of `nj_mean` to `nj_min`, the truncated-gamma generator
reaches every `cv` from 0 up to a limit. The limit is about 1.43 when the mean
is ten times the minimum, 1.11 at five times, and 0.57 at twice. Above the
limit `sim_multisite()` stops with an error, and it warns when `nj_mean` is
less than twice `nj_min`.

## Standard errors set directly

`sim_meta()` takes no site sizes. It builds the standard errors from two
numbers. `I` is the informativeness,
$I = \sigma_\tau^2 / (\sigma_\tau^2 + \mathrm{GM})$, where $\mathrm{GM}$ is
the geometric mean of the sampling variances. It lies between 0 and 1, and it
is larger when the standard errors are small relative to the cross-site
standard deviation $\sigma_\tau$. `R` is the heterogeneity ratio, the largest
sampling variance divided by the smallest. With `R = 1`, the default, all
sites have the same standard error.

The function solves the first definition for the geometric mean,
$\mathrm{GM} = \sigma_\tau^2 (1 - I) / I$. It then places the $J$ sampling
variances at equal steps on the log scale from $\mathrm{GM} / \sqrt{R}$ to
$\mathrm{GM} \sqrt{R}$.

```{r direct}
meta <- sim_meta(J = 50, I = 0.3, R = 2, sigma_tau = 0.2, seed = 1)
meta
round(range(meta$se2_j), 4)
```

The last header line gives the target and the realized informativeness, both
0.300. The geometric mean is $0.2^2 \times 0.7 / 0.3 = 0.0933$, and the
sampling variances run from 0.066 to 0.132, a ratio of 2. The `n_j` column is
`NA` because there are no site sizes.

`gen_se_direct()` runs this step alone on the output of `gen_effects()`.

```{r direct-step}
set.seed(1)
effects <- gen_effects(J = 10, sigma_tau = 0.2)
gen_se_direct(effects, J = 10, I = 0.3, R = 2, sigma_tau = 0.2, shuffle = FALSE)
```

With `shuffle = FALSE` the sampling variances rise with the site index, from
0.0660 to 0.132. With `shuffle = TRUE`, the default, the same values go to the
sites in random order. `se_fn` takes a function of `J` that returns a list
with the sampling variances `se2_j` and, optionally, the sizes `n_j`, which
are then used as they are (`I` must still be given). `sim_meta()` accepts both
arguments.

## Which one to use

Derive the standard errors from site sizes when the simulation stands for a
trial. You then say how large the sites are, how unequal, what share is
treated, and what the covariates explain, and the precision follows. The
informativeness and the heterogeneity ratio are results, and they change from
one data set to the next.

```{r seeds}
round(sapply(1:5, function(seed) {
  d <- sim_multisite(
    J = 50, nj_mean = 50, cv = 0.5, nj_min = 10, R2 = 0.4, seed = seed
  )
  c(I = informativeness(d), R = heterogeneity_ratio(d$se2_j))
}), 3)
```

Over seeds 1 to 5 the informativeness stays between 0.420 and 0.434, and the
heterogeneity ratio runs from 4.810 to 10.538.

Set the standard errors directly when the precision itself is what you know
or want to control. In a meta-analysis the studies report estimates and
standard errors, and their sample sizes are often missing or not comparable.
A simulation study may need the same informativeness in every data set.
`sim_meta()` returns the same set of standard errors for every seed and
changes only which site gets which. Each function rejects the arguments of the
other.

`I` and `R` fix the geometric mean of the sampling variances and the ratio of
the largest to the smallest, not how the values are spread in between. The
last example asks `sim_meta()` for the `I` and `R` of `dat`.

```{r compare, fig.height = 2.5, fig.cap = "The standard errors set directly are evenly spaced on the log scale, and those from site sizes are not."}
direct <- sim_meta(
  J = 50, I = informativeness(dat), R = heterogeneity_ratio(dat$se2_j), seed = 1
)
both <- rbind(
  data.frame(source = "from site sizes", se_j = dat$se_j),
  data.frame(source = "set directly", se_j = direct$se_j)
)
ggplot(both, aes(se_j, source)) +
  geom_point(shape = "|", size = 6) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(x = "standard error (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Each mark is the standard error of one site, and both rows have the same
informativeness and heterogeneity ratio. Most of the standard errors from
site sizes lie close together below 0.3, and those of a few small sites stand
apart above it. If that shape matters, derive the standard errors from site
sizes or supply them through `se_fn`.
